1. Core Clinical Tension: A 60-year-old immunocompetent woman from Uttar Pradesh presented with a high-grade fever of 6 weeks' duration, pancytopenia, marked hepatosplenomegaly, and hypergammaglobulinemia, concurrently accompanied by extensive noduloulcerative cutaneous lesions across the face and trunk, anterior uveitis, and jaundice. The combination of simultaneous visceral, cutaneous, and ocular manifestations in an HIV-negative host created strong diagnostic overlap with disseminated histoplasmosis, lepromatous leprosy, or systemic vasculitis.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission clinical triage ends after bedside fundoscopy, triage laboratories (CBC demonstrating pancytopenia, LFTs showing cholestatic jaundice and hypoalbuminemia, high IgG), and abdominal ultrasound demonstrating hepatosplenomegaly, immediately before invasive diagnostic biopsies (skin, liver, bone marrow).
3. Differential Distinctions: Disseminated histoplasmosis and mycobacterial infections (tuberculosis, lepromatous leprosy) were primary differential considerations for multi-organ reticuloendothelial, cutaneous, and ocular involvement, while autoimmune disease/vasculitis was considered for the arthralgias and uveitis. The diagnostic pivot was the demonstration of intracellular Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies/amastigotes on skin, liver, and bone marrow biopsies, confirming disseminated visceral and mucocutaneous leishmaniasis.
case_prompt:
A 60-year-old woman hailing from eastern Uttar Pradesh, India, presented with a 6-week history of high-grade continuous fever associated with chills, rigors, anorexia, malaise, polyarthralgias, and severe lethargy. Concurrent with her fevers, she noted successive crops of round, raised cutaneous lesions that began on the left upper limb, spread to the right upper limb, and progressively involved the face, upper back, chest, and upper abdomen. Some lesions enlarged into nodules with central depressions draining purulent material, accompanied by erythema and pain. One week prior to admission, she developed jaundice and mild-to-moderate right upper quadrant abdominal pain, without pruritus, acholic stools, or bleeding. She also developed progressive, symmetrical, painless bilateral lower-extremity edema without facial puffiness or oliguria, alongside painful red eyes, nodular lesions of the eyelids and conjunctiva, and decreased visual acuity. She was a teetotaler with no prior comorbidities, and took no immunosuppressive medications or corticosteroids.

On physical examination, body temperature was 100.8°F (38.2°C), pulse was 100 beats per minute, and blood pressure was 128/88 mmHg. She demonstrated pronounced pallor and scleral icterus without peripheral lymphadenopathy, clubbing, or cyanosis. Bilateral pedal pitting edema was present. Cutaneous examination revealed multiple crops of shiny nodular, papular, and noduloulcerative lesions across the face and upper torso, some exhibiting central purulent drainage. Ophthalmic examination showed nodular lesions over the eyelids and conjunctiva with conjunctival injection; bedside fundoscopy revealed features of uveitis and small retinal hemorrhages. Abdominal examination demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly without ascites.

Initial laboratory evaluation revealed hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL (normocytic normochromic anemia), leukocyte count 5,600/mm³, platelet count 80,000/mm³, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 80 mm/1st h. Liver biochemistries showed total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL (direct fraction 1.8 mg/dL), AST 50 IU/L, ALT 60 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 IU/L, GGT 150 IU/L, serum albumin 1.9 g/dL, and INR 1.3. Serum IgG was elevated at 22.6 g/L. Serologies for HIV-1/2, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody were non-reactive. Chest radiography was normal. Abdominal imaging confirmed hepatosplenomegaly without ascites, intrahepatic biliary dilatation, or abdominal lymphadenopathy.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given the triad of chronic fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, marked hypergammaglobulinemia, and disseminated ulcerative skin lesions with ocular involvement; ruled out by histopathology demonstrating amastigotes with kinetoplasts (Leishman-Donovan bodies) within macrophages rather than narrow-based budding yeast cells.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The dermis showed loss of adnexal structures and a rich collection of histiocytes filled with amastigote forms of leishmaniasis (Figure 2(a)).

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Systemic autoimmune vasculitis or Lupus erythematosus
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the combination of polyarthralgias, widespread facial eruptions, cytopenias, ocular inflammation (uveitis, retinal hemorrhages), and marked hypergammaglobulinemia; ruled out by histopathological identification of intracellular protozoal parasites within histiocytic infiltrates across skin, liver, and bone marrow.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A fundoscopy performed at the bedside revealed features of uveitis and small retinal hemorrhages... The hyperplastic Kupffer cells and granulomatous collection of macrophages showed presence of intracellular LD bodies (Figure 2(b)) which was also subsequently shown in the bone marrow biopsy (Figure 3).

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Diagnostic Pivot: Disseminated Leishmaniasis (concurrent visceral, mucocutaneous, and ocular involvement)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Skin biopsy of the back lesion, ultrasound-guided liver biopsy, and bone marrow biopsy all demonstrated dense macrophage infiltration loaded with intracellular Leishman-Donovan (LD) amastigote bodies, establishing multivisceral and disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis, followed by clinical recovery on liposomal amphotericin B and miltefosine.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The dermis showed loss of adnexal structures and a rich collection of histiocytes filled with amastigote forms of leishmaniasis (Figure 2(a)). The liver biopsy revealed the presence of acinar disarray with hepatocytes showing ballooning degeneration, mild steatosis, and glycogenated nuclei. Several foci of lobular inflammation and prominence of hyperplastic Kupffer cells were noted with formation of few small granulomas. The hyperplastic Kupffer cells and granulomatous collection of macrophages showed presence of intracellular LD bodies (Figure 2(b)) which was also subsequently shown in the bone marrow biopsy (Figure 3).

editor_comments: Concurrent presentation of visceral leishmaniasis with disseminated mucocutaneous and ocular involvement in an immunocompetent, HIV-negative patient is extraordinarily rare. Demonstration of LD bodies in multiple tissues (skin, liver, bone marrow) provided definitive confirmation.
